title: Fat Bear Week Returns: 16 Bears, One Very Round Crown
summary:
Every fall, thousands of people stare at photos of very large brown bears and argue about which one is the fattest. This is not a joke — it's Fat Bear Week, and it's now in its 12th year. From September 22 to September 29, fans worldwide vote online for the chubbiest bear at Katmai National Park in Alaska.

Katmai spans 4.1 million acres of volcanoes, rivers, and forests, and it's home to roughly 2,200 brown bears. There are no roads into the park — visitors arrive by boat or plane. The bears bulk up on salmon from the park's rivers, packing on fat reserves that carry them through the long Alaskan winter.

The contest started small. In 2014, Park Ranger Mike Fitz noticed two photos of the same bear on the park's website, taken months apart by a bear camera. The difference in size was astonishing. Fitz and other rangers turned it into a one-day Facebook event called "Fat Bear Tuesday," where votes were counted as "likes." The next year, it expanded into a full week. By 2025, more than 1.7 million votes poured in from over 100 countries.

The format is a single-elimination bracket. Each day, fans pick between two bears. The winner advances; the loser is out. Rounds continue until two bears remain, and the final vote on September 29 crowns the champion.

This year's bracket has 16 bears, each with a story. Bear 32, known as Chunk, is the defending 2025 champion and is back after recovering from a broken jaw. Bear 164, or Bucky, became a fan favorite this summer for snatching leaping salmon out of the air. Bear 132 is competing while raising three cubs — one of whom got separated from the family and survived alone for several days before reuniting. And Bear 806 is raising her own cub alongside an adopted young bear named Biggie.

It's silly, sure. But it's also a reminder of why protecting wild places like Katmai matters.
why_it_matters: It shows how a joke can become a serious tool: online contests can convert public attention into support for conservation, at a time when protecting huge wild areas depends on people who may never see them in person.

background_read: Katmai National Park was first protected as a national monument after a huge volcanic eruption in 1912 buried the valley in ash, and it later became a full national park.
The rivers inside it support one of the world's largest salmon runs, which is exactly why so many brown bears gather there to feed before the long Alaska winter.

Fat Bear Week is run by the U.S. National Park Service (the government agency that manages America's national parks) together with explore.org, a charity that runs live wildlife webcams so people anywhere can watch the bears online.

The contest is a modern kind of conservation campaign: it turns animal behaviour into an internet game, and the attention it earns helps make the case for protecting wild land that most of the people voting will never visit.
The bears' survival still depends on healthy salmon runs, which face pressure from warming rivers and from large development plans in the region.

perspectives.description: A playful contest draws millions of eyes to a remote park with no roads and no easy way to advertise itself. That attention can translate into donations, volunteers, and political goodwill for protecting the land and its salmon runs.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — those worried about the bears themselves
perspectives.description: The framing rewards bears for being visible and close to the falls, and it makes a serious biological event — packing on weight to survive winter — look like pure entertainment. Underneath the fun, the bears are only as healthy as the salmon runs, which are under real pressure.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — analysts of internet science communication
perspectives.description: Fat Bear Week fits a well-known pattern: crowdsourced voting brackets, livestreamed animals, and named individuals turn slow ecological processes into something people can follow daily. It works because it asks for almost nothing — a click — while building familiarity over years.

The bigger test is whether the contest's audience stays engaged after the votes are counted, and whether that energy reaches decisions about rivers, fishing, and development. If the salmon runs shrink, the fattest-bear bracket will have a much sadder story behind it.
